image_description: A group of sea lions in a turquoise pool within an enclosure. One sea lion is swimming with its head and upper torso visible in the center background, facing forward. Another sea lion's head is visible on the right side, partially submerged. On the left, several sea lions are hauled out on rocks, appearing as dark, rounded shapes. The background shows a concrete edge, some rocks, and fencing.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Head is broad with prominent sagittal crest in males.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The central sea lion's head is visible but appears smooth; no distinct sagittal crest is clearly identifiable due to image resolution and wet fur, though the head shape is broadly consistent with a pinniped.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: External ear pinnae (visible ear flaps) distinguish from true seals.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: While sea lions have external ears, they are small and often difficult to see in low-resolution images or when wet. No clear ear flap is distinctly visible on the central subject, making this checkpoint fail strict visibility criteria.
Image resolution is too low to resolve individual whiskers. They are not visibly prominent.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Fur is short and coarse ranging from brown to dark grey, lighter on ventral surface.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible fur on the swimming sea lion and the hauled-out ones matches the description: dark brown/grey, appearing sleek/wet which implies short/coarse texture typical of otariids.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body exhibits streamlined fusiform form of substantial marine mammal proportions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The central subject displays a classic streamlined, torpedo-like body shape consistent with a sea lion.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Males develop thick neck mane and are significantly larger than females.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: It is impossible to determine sex or compare sizes accurately between the submerged/swimming individuals and those on the rocks. No obvious mane is visible on the central figure.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Foreflippers are large, broad, and hairless on underside used for terrestrial locomotion.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The foreflippers of the swimming sea lion are underwater or obscured by the body angle. The hauled-out sea lions are too distant/blurry to inspect flipper details.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Hind flippers can rotate forward for walking on land.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Hind flippers are not visible on any subject; they are either underwater or obscured by the body/rocks.
The visible portion of the central sea lion shows symmetrical alignment of the head and shoulders.
